summary: Updates the Internet Message Format, RFC 5322, to allow group syntax in the From and Sender header fields, and also Resent-From and Resent-Sender, in certain situations. Before, groups were allowed only in fields like To and Cc.

eli5.summary: An email says who it is from. This lets that spot name a whole team instead of just one person.

subtitle: Email's From: and Sender: headers may now use group syntax, mainly so a message can say it has no address to reply to.

tldr.problem: The Internet Message Format required a usable mailbox in From: and Sender:, but automated senders and internationalized addresses sometimes have no address that can be replied to.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6854 changes the From: and Sender: syntax to accept the existing group form, including an empty group such as From: Automated System:; and applies the same change to Resent-From: and Resent-Sender:.
tldr.outcome: Groups are now legal in these fields, but the RFC says user agents SHOULD NOT let people use them in outgoing messages, so the mailbox form stays the normal choice.

facts.label: Sender with group
facts.value: At most one mailbox in the group

today: RFC 6854 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2013 that updates RFC 5322. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why From: Needed to Change
sections.content:
Ever since RFC 822, the Internet Message Format has required a usable address in the From: field so that replies can be sent. RFC 5322 kept that rule: the originator fields (From: and Sender:) had to use the mailbox form and could not use the group form, which allows an empty list of addresses.

The RFC says the use cases have changed. Some automated systems want to send email but cannot handle replies. And work on internationalized email addresses (RFC 6530) creates a need to hand a message with an internationalized address to an older client that cannot reply to it but can still display it. A group with an empty list gives an existing syntax for an unusable address, plus a text label describing the originator.

The author reviewed many current email programs and found that all reviewed clients properly display a message with group syntax in From:. At worst they show an error when you try to reply.
sections.eli5: Some senders, like a robot, cannot read replies. This RFC lets a message say so by naming a group with nobody in it.

sections.title: The Syntax Change
sections.content:
RFC 6854 replaces Section 3.6.2 of RFC 5322. The From: field now takes either a mailbox-list or an address-list, the same element used by To:, CC: and Reply-To:. The Sender: field now takes either a mailbox or an address. Since an address already includes a mailbox, spelling out both is a way of highlighting that the change is meant for limited use.

Section 2.2 makes the matching change to Resent-From: and Resent-Sender: in Section 3.6.6 of RFC 5322. Only the ABNF changes there; the rest of that section stays as it was.

The rules around the fields mostly carry over. If From: holds more than one mailbox (counting mailboxes inside groups), a Sender: field with a single address MUST appear. If Sender: uses group syntax, the group MUST NOT contain more than one mailbox. Without a Reply-To: field, replies SHOULD by default go to the mailboxes in From:.
sections.eli5: The rule for the 'from' line used to say 'a person'. Now it says 'a person or a group', the same as the 'to' line.

sections.title: Limited Use: The Applicability Statement
sections.content:
Mailbox syntax stays the normal syntax for From: and Sender:. The group form is only for Limited Use, as defined in RFC 2026 (RFC 2026).

The reason is that much email software assumes the addresses in these fields can be replied to and are suitable for organizing and filtering mail. Groups can disrupt that. So the RFC legitimizes groups only for circumstances where they are necessary, asks that they be used with caution, and states that user agents SHOULD NOT permit the use of groups in those fields in outgoing messages.

The updated RFC 5322 text also says the From: field SHOULD use only the mailbox-list syntax and the Sender: field SHOULD use only mailbox syntax.

The change makes groups legal, but the RFC recommends against their general use in these fields.
sections.eli5: You are allowed to use the new group spot, but only when you really have to. Normally you should still put one real person.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples. First, an automated nightly monitor program whose replies should not be sent. Today such messages often carry a valid address that discards replies, so people who reply may not know that their replies vanish. With group syntax the email client will not allow a reply in the first place:

From: Nightly Monitor Robot:;

Second, a message meant to be from two managing partners, Ben and Carol, but sent by their assistant, Dave. It could always be written with two mailboxes in From: and Dave in Sender:. The change allows the partners to be named as a group:

From: Managing Partners:ben@example.com,carol@example.com;
Sender: dave@example.com
sections.eli5: A robot can sign its note 'Nightly Monitor Robot' with no mailbox, so nobody can reply to it. Two bosses can sign as 'Managing Partners'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most user agents display the From: address, or its friendly text, as the origin of the message. Group syntax can hide the identity of the originator. The RFC argues that a fabricated From: address does the same job, so allowing groups does not make that problem worse.

Protocols that match the From: address to a verified domain, such as the ADSP document (RFC 5617), cannot apply to messages with no actual address in From:. Local policy decides how those are handled, so senders need to know that using groups might hurt deliverability.

Some RFC 5322 implementations might not expect groups in these fields, and a subset might behave in an exploitable way. The RFC considers this unlikely to be a serious problem, because address parsers are required to understand group syntax and because attackers can already violate RFC 5322.
sections.eli5: A group name can hide who really sent a message, but a made-up address can do that too. Some spam checks also need a real address, so group senders may get their mail blocked.

sections.title: IANA Registry Update
sections.content: IANA updated the Permanent Message Header Field Names registry. The entries for From, Sender, Resent-From and Resent-Sender now cite both RFC 5322 and RFC 6854 as references. Nothing else about the entries changed.
sections.eli5: The official list of header names now points to this new rule as well as the old one.
